pr_title: sd-boot: Add support to boot last select entry
pr_comments:
I reworked this to use an EFI var instead. It can also be set with bootctl now too and given how the code is now, listing the last booted entry in print_status is trivial now.

There already exists the volatile LoaderEntrySelected var which I could've reused for this. But there is some silly requirement that requires deleting the var first before you can change its attributes (volatile vs non-volatile), which I felt would over-complicate things.

issue_context.title: systemd-boot: allow to default to the last booted entry
issue_context.body:
I dual-boot between Windows 10 and Arch Linux. Sometimes Windows wants to reboot without asking after installing the updates. I would still like to be greeted by the Windows login screen after this, not Linux. On the other hand, after rebooting Linux, I would still like to get back into Linux by default.

It would be nice if I could configure systemd-boot (via loader.conf) so that it automatically remembers (without having to press "d") which entry was booted last, and boot into that by default.

E.g.:

default=last-booted-entry

Note: I am not asking to make this "remember the last booted entry" behavior the default. I am asking to make it possible.

Obviously there is some interaction with boot-blessing logic, but, as I don't use this logic, I can't think of a good design here. Maybe we'll also need some logic that prevents certain entries from being remembered, not sure here.

Systemd version that doesn't have this feature: 247
comments:
hmm, so far we refrained from doing automatic persistent efi variable changes in "regular" boot code paths, and instead only in case where the user explicitly reconfigures something, because the involved memory chips are typically low quality and the memory management implementations for persistent efi vars in firmware even worse, hence making changes on every single boot is a bit questionnable.

That said, I figure as an option we can certainly add that. And maybe quality of the firmware implementations and memory chips has increased today. And if you don't update your kernel that often/change what to boot into the write cycles don't grow thaaaat much.

review_comments: given that we don't trust the EFI fs drivers too much I think we should make sure we really really have to update things before we make changes to disk. i.e. reading from disk should be less problematic than writing hence supress writing if the file already has the right contents.
That's what the very first if in this function is for (entry_default_pattern is what we've read previously).
Quite frankly, I'd love to use the rust approach inside of boot.c: a helper to allocate+assert. It's not like there's anything sensible to be done in these cases...

Also, in this particular case, an allocation failure is non-fatal. We'd end up deleting the var instead of setting it, but no cats will be killed in the process. But this is a nice example of me wondering what to do here: should this be treated as fatal or not. If yes, then an assert approach would serve us just as well while keeping the code nicer imho.

I would be fine with allocators which abort on failure I think. Unlike in Linux userspace we "own" the machine fully after all, and thus if we can't work there's not much benefit in handling it graceful: we have one important job and if that job cannot be fulfilled it's fatal anyway for the whole system...
